summary: Metalink/HTTP puts download mirror locations, peer-to-peer sources, cryptographic hashes, and signatures in HTTP header fields. These are normally in an XML Metalink file. Download tools can use this to pick mirrors and verify files.

eli5.summary: When you download a file, the server can also say where else you can get it and give a fingerprint to check it. This puts that information in the reply headers.

questions: how to specify mirrors and hashes in http
how do http link headers list mirrors
what is the digest header in metalink
what is a preferred mirror in metalink
subtitle: Mirror lists, hashes and signatures for a download, carried in ordinary HTTP response headers.

tldr.problem: A file is often available from many mirrors, but users must pick one by hand, a slow or broken mirror is only discovered mid-download, and a corrupted file is hard to repair.
tldr.mechanism: The server answers with Link header fields that list mirrors, peer-to-peer metadata and signatures, plus a Digest header field holding a cryptographic hash of the whole file. Clients use these to choose sources, download in parallel and verify the result.
tldr.outcome: A client can fall back to other mirrors, detect mismatched or corrupt data, and verify the finished file. A shared ETag or Digest on mirrors does not protect against a determined attacker, so the whole-file hash from the Metalink server is what the client relies on.

today: RFC 6249 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2011. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem and the Idea
sections.content:
Identical copies of a file often sit on many servers, reachable over FTP, HTTP or peer-to-peer. Users are usually shown a list of these mirrors and must choose one by hand. They rarely have enough information to choose well, so they often pick the first, which gives that server a disproportionate share of the load. A slow, outdated or unreachable server is only discovered after the download starts, and a corrupted transfer has no easy repair.

The RFC notes that DNS load balancing can balance long-term server load fairly effectively, but it is less effective at delivering the best throughput when the bottleneck is the network rather than the server. A plain HTTP redirect to a mirror carries only one link to one server, and HTTP has no provision for handling failures.

Metalink/HTTP is the alternative: put the information normally found in a Metalink XML file (RFC 5854) into HTTP header fields, reusing existing standards: Web Linking (RFC 5988), Instance Digests in HTTP (RFC 3230) and ETags from RFC 2616. The collection of header fields is called a Metalink.
sections.eli5: Instead of making you pick a shop from a long list, the server tells your computer about all the shops and a way to check the goods. Your computer then chooses for you.

sections.title: What Servers and Clients Must Do
sections.content:
A Metalink server is an HTTP server that provides a Metalink in its response header fields. It MUST support Link header fields for listing mirrors and Instance Digests, and it MUST return the same Link header fields and Instance Digests on HEAD requests. Every Metalink MUST include a whole-file hash using SHA-256, and it MAY include other hashes.

Metalink servers and their preferred mirrors MUST share the same ETag policy: byte-for-byte identical files get the same ETag on the mirror as on the Metalink server. The RFC suggests deriving an ETag from a cryptographic hash of the file contents rather than from server-specific filesystem metadata. Servers SHOULD also offer Metalink/XML documents with hashes of parts of the file if error recovery is wanted.

Mirror servers SHOULD support partial content. Clients MUST support HTTP, SHOULD support FTP, and MAY support BitTorrent or other methods. Clients MUST support Instance Digests by requesting and verifying hashes, SHOULD switch mirrors when one becomes unreachable, and SHOULD check digital signatures. A client MUST discard Link header fields that come from a mirror or that list the Metalink server itself, to prevent an infinite loop.
sections.eli5: The main server must always give a fingerprint of the file. Helper servers should give the same label to the same file, and your computer must check the fingerprint at the end and not follow the helpers' own lists of helpers.

sections.title: Mirrors and Their Attributes
sections.content:
Mirrors are listed in Link header fields with the relation type duplicate, which this RFC registers. Four optional attributes describe each mirror.

  • pri: priority, from 1 to 999999. A lower value means higher priority, and a mirror with no pri counts as 999999, the lowest. Clients SHOULD use lower values first but MAY choose otherwise.
  • geo: an ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country code for the physical server, which a client MAY use to pick mirrors that are geographically near.
  • pref: marks a preferred mirror, an HTTP mirror that shares the ETag policy of the Metalink server or, if ETags are not used, provides an Instance Digest with the same algorithm. Mirrors without it are normal mirrors. FTP mirrors are always normal.
  • depth: how much of the path is mirrored. The default depth=0 means only that file. A value of 1 means the file and everything in its rightmost path segment, and each higher value adds one path segment closer to the host.

It is up to the organization how many Link header fields the server provides. The RFC suggests this could be a random selection or a hard limit based on factors such as network proximity, file size or server load. Priority is purely the server's preference; the client decides what to do with it.
sections.eli5: Each helper shop on the list can come with a note: how much we like it, which country it is in, whether it labels things the same way we do, and how many aisles of stock it copies.

sections.title: Other Links: Peer-to-Peer, Metalink XML and Signatures
sections.content:
Besides mirrors, the same Link header field can point to descriptions of the file using the relation type describedby and a type parameter giving the MIME type. A .torrent file uses application/x-bittorrent. A Metalink/XML file uses application/metalink4+xml. An optional name attribute names the file described inside a metainfo file, because the name there may differ from the one on the Metalink server. Clients MAY use metainfo files for downloading.

Metalink/XML files are particularly useful because they can carry hashes of parts of a file. Servers SHOULD provide them and clients SHOULD use them for error recovery.

Signatures are also linked with describedby. An OpenPGP signature (RFC 3156) uses type application/pgp-signature, and an S/MIME signature (RFC 5751) uses application/pkcs7-mime. Clients SHOULD support both.

The whole-file hash travels in the Digest header field. If Instance Digests are not provided by the Metalink server, the Link header fields pertaining to this specification MUST be ignored.
sections.eli5: The server can also point to a torrent, a detailed checklist for parts of the file, and a signed note proving who made it. The fingerprint of the whole file comes in the reply too.

sections.title: How a Multi-Source Download Works
sections.content:
The client starts with an ordinary GET to the Metalink server, optionally with a range limit, or with a HEAD request to learn the mirrors first. The response carries the data plus mirror locations, the Instance Digest, the ETag, the size from Content-Length, any Metalink/XML link, peer-to-peer information and signatures.

The client then asks a preferred mirror for a byte range, sending an If-Match header with the ETag. If the file is the same, the mirror replies 206 Partial Content. Clients SHOULD use preferred mirrors where possible because of this early mismatch check, and SHOULD send the original GET location in Referer.

Clients MAY open parallel range requests to several mirrors, but MUST limit the number of parallel connections, ideally by watching whether aggregate throughput rises when a connection is added. They MUST NOT make more than one concurrent request to each mirror for a given file. Clients SHOULD close all but the fastest connection if a range request gets a complete response instead of a partial one, SHOULD abort extremely slow or stalled requests and finish them elsewhere, and can split the final range among several mirrors. If the first request was a GET without a Range header, the first connection is sacrificed when the client catches up; a HEAD first avoids that.

A client MUST reject downloads from mirrors whose file size does not match the Metalink server, and MUST reject a mirror's download if its Instance Digest uses the same algorithm but a different value. When the download finishes the client MUST verify the whole-file hash. Clients that verify digital signatures MUST verify those included, and they MUST validate back to a trust anchor.
sections.eli5: Your computer grabs different chunks from different helpers at the same time, but not too many at once. At the end it checks the fingerprint of the whole file.

sections.title: Preventing and Fixing Errors
sections.content:
The RFC separates three jobs. Prevention (early mismatch detection) uses file sizes, ETags and Instance Digests before data moves. Detection uses the Instance Digest after the transfer. Correction uses hashes of parts of the file. Hashes from Instance Digests are base64; those in Metalink/XML are hexadecimal.

Merged ranges SHOULD be checked against a strong validator, either an Instance Digest or an ETag shared with a preferred mirror. A mirror that gives a matching shared ETag or Digest passes early; one that provides neither cannot be checked early unless the file length also differs. The RFC states that ETags cannot be used to verify content integrity; they only tell the client that the responses are assumed valid for that object. They prevent accidental merging of ranges from different versions of a file with the same name.

If the final hash does not match the Instance Digest from the Metalink server, the client SHOULD fetch the Metalink/XML file if available. Its partial hashes show which mirror returned bad data and which ranges can be kept and which must be fetched again. If the download cannot be repaired it is corrupt, and the client can try again.
sections.eli5: Checking at the start tells you if you are grabbing the wrong version. Checking at the end tells you if anything got scrambled, and a detailed checklist shows which piece to fetch again.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A shared ETag or Instance Digest cannot strictly protect against malicious attacks or server or network errors replacing content, because an attacker can make a mirror appear to return the expected values. The client therefore relies on the Instance Digest from the Metalink server in the first response to verify the whole object.

Spoofing is possible: an attacker can publish Metalinks with false information to trick downloaders into fetching a malicious or worthless file, and malicious publishers could insert unrelated URIs to attempt a distributed denial-of-service attack (RFC 4732). As with all downloads, users should download only from trusted sources.

Some digest values from RFC 3230, including the whole Message Digest family, are considered insecure because of collisions, so a malicious file could match the intended file's hash. This is why SHA-256 is required. Metalinks SHOULD include digital signatures, which provide authentication and message integrity and enable non-repudiation with proof of origin.
sections.eli5: A liar can pretend to have the right label, so the fingerprint from the main server and a signed note are what you really trust.

messages.label: GET (or HEAD)
messages.note: An ordinary request, optionally with a range limit.

messages.label: 200 OK + Link, Digest, ETag
messages.note: Mirror list, whole-file hash, ETag and size.

messages.label: GET with Range and If-Match
messages.note: Asks for part of the file if the ETag matches.

messages.label: 206 Partial Content
messages.note: Returns the range with ETag and Instance Digest.

viz.caption: OPTIONAL ATTRIBUTES OF A MIRROR LINK

items.label: Priority
items.desc: 1 to 999999; lower is higher priority; default 999999.

items.label: Location
items.desc: ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country code of the server.

items.label: Preferred mirror
items.desc: HTTP mirror sharing the ETag policy or Digest algorithm.

items.label: Mirror depth
items.desc: Path segments mirrored; 0 (default) means only that file.
